@C_Barraud's Tuesday Brief has an interesting chart from JPMorgan Asset Management (via @dailychartbook): “History shows that large market moves are often followed by meaningful moves in the opposite direction.”

The data backs that up, with a catch (and scroll down further for what historically comes next):
▪️ Nine of the 10 historical moves on JPMorgan’s chart reversed the next day. Only March 24, 2020 didn’t.
▪️ But every one of them came with the S&P 500 already 16% to 46% below its high, consistent with typical big swings in both directions in bear markets: 17 of the 20 biggest up days since 1950 came 20% or more off the high, and none came within 10% of one.
▪️ In that regard, a big up day isn’t an all-clear. After the 11.6% gain on October 13, 2008, the index fell another 33% over the next year.

Last Thursday’s 4.4% drop started just 1.7% below the October 6 record, which is a different setup. Since 1950, a 4% one-day drop from within 5% of a record has happened only five other times:
▪️ September 1955 (Eisenhower’s heart attack), September 1986, October 1989 (Friday-the-13th mini-crash), October 1997 (the Asian crisis) and February 2018 (Volmageddon).
▪️ All five were higher three and six months later. Four of five were higher a year later, with 1989 the exception.
▪️ New record closes came 39 to 228 days later, with a median of 82.
▪️ The catch: 1989 and 2018, the two slowest to recover, both fell about 11% further along the way.

Also note this time the second big move came with a day's delay with Friday’s 0.3% gain before Monday’s 2.35% gain. The two days won back 59% of Thursday’s drop. That’s at the strong end of those five cases: 1955 won back 56% and 1997 65%, while 2018 won back only 29%. The S&P 500 is now 3.4% below its record.

The timing lesson holds: JPMorgan AM finds 7 of the 10 best days from 2005 to 2024 came within two weeks of one of the 10 worst. Selling into a shock usually means missing a rebound.

Also note it’s a small sample, so it's certainly not guaranteed.

Tuesday’s CPI is the last before the Fed’s December 8th–9th meeting. Bloomberg consensus is 0.3% for headline and 0.2% for core, after 0.65% and 0.33% in September (core’s most since April).

Five bank forecasts (headline / core / core PCE):

▪️ Goldman Sachs: 0.21% / 0.16% / 0.23%.

▪️ Morgan Stanley: 0.19% / 0.19% / 0.22%.

▪️ Bank of America: 0.17% / 0.22% / 0.23%.

▪️ Barclays: 0.24% / 0.22% / 0.21%.

▪️ JPMorgan: 0.25% / 0.23% / 0.23%.

All five core calls round to the 0.2% consensus, but four of five see headline below 0.3%. The core PCE readthrough is 0.21% to 0.23%, which BofA and JPMorgan say would push core PCE back up to 3.2% y/y.

Where they agree:
▪️ Shelter should cool. Owners’ equivalent rent jumped 0.35% in September, which Morgan Stanley calls “largely noise, amplified by unusual volatility in the Midwest,” and Goldman, BofA and JPMorgan all see 0.26% to 0.3%.

▪️ AI is showing up in goods prices. BofA says IT commodities added roughly 90bp to core goods’ 2.4% annualized three-month pace, and Morgan Stanley cites “AI-related price pressures.”

▪️A December hike is likely. BofA says its forecast “would effectively lock in another 25bp hike,” and that it would take “an indisputably soft 0.1% m/m print” to change the Fed’s mind. Barclays sees October as “a pause, rather than a reversal."  JPM says "a very
soft number could raise questions about a hike next month, but that is not our expectation," and a third straight 0.3% would challenge market pricing for only one more hike next year. Morgan Stanley expects hikes in December and March. 

Where they disagree:
▪️ Health insurance gets its semiannual source-data update. Goldman and JPMorgan see about −2.5%, BofA −0.9%, while Barclays expects a firmer run-rate.

▪️ Used cars: Goldman sees −1.5% based on auction prices, BofA flat and JPMorgan +0.4%.

▪️ Energy: BofA sees −0.38%, while Goldman and JPMorgan see +0.5%.

An Unprecedented Whipsaw in Investor 'Fear'

The VIX fell 22% Monday to 19.93, its biggest drop since April 2025. That came after Thursday’s 70% jump, which followed a 20% drop Wednesday.

Since 1990, that’s the only time the VIX has fallen 20%+ within three sessions on both sides of a 30%+ jump. 

You have to loosen it to 15% drops to find another case: Brexit.

▪ June 23, 2016 (vote day): VIX −18.5% as markets bet on Remain.
▪ June 24 (Leave wins): VIX +49%, S&P 500 −3.6%, pound −8% to its lowest since 1985.
▪ June 28: VIX −21%.
▪ What happened next: S&P 500 at a record 11 sessions after the vote, up 6.6% a month later. VIX at a two-year low by August.

One key difference: in 2016, the 10-year hit a record low and the Fed pushed off rate hikes.

As promised, here’s my setup for cross-channel analytics ↓

https://t.co/dRaWjAst9l

TL;DR:

→ Components

Google Sheets = database: one spreadsheet for content, plus separate spreadsheets for paid placements, zero-cost marketing experiments, and SEO.

Typefully = a list of published posts via API, including full text and tags.

GA4 (+ Search Console) = traffic and sign-ups on the newsletter site, by page and source.

n8n = glue. A workflow runs twice a week, collects new posts from every platform, labels them, and writes snapshots into Sheets.

Claude built most of the above with me: it labels posts, loads the weekly exports, writes the weekly analysis, and builds the dashboard (I also have it as an artefact for visualisation).

Native exports: Substack (subscribers, traffic sources, growth sources), Telegram channel statistics, and X analytics CSVs.

→ The workflow

Twice a week (Monday and Thursday morning), the n8n workflow pulls new posts: the Substack archive and notes, the public web page of the Telegram channel, and published drafts from Typefully. Every new post gets a row.

A model suggests a topic (one of 12 marketing directions, e.g., SEO / SMM / Strategy), a format for newsletter issues, and a post type based on the desired target action—e.g., discovery (main goal: maximise shares) or resource (main goal: link clicks). I review the labels once a week and correct them. Edited copies of the same post on other platforms are detected automatically and inherit the original labels.

At 7 days and 30 days, the workflow writes a metrics row for each post. Public numbers (likes, restacks, views, reactions) come in automatically. Private ones are added by hand from screenshots.

On Monday, I drop the Telegram, X, and Substack exports into a Claude chat. Claude loads them into the right tabs, checks the totals against the files, and writes a short summary of the week.

A single page reads the sheets and shows trends, top posts relative to a typical post on that platform, article promotion windows, and a “this week” to-do list.

Full breakdown → https://t.co/XUkqpncnbR

🇨🇳 China's exports surged 35.2% YoY in October with high-tech exports up 66.6% and integrated circuits jumping 137.1%. Impressive numbers but a rather worrying economic paradox lies.

📊 High-tech products now account for nearly 34% of China's total exports and explain roughly 52% of their annual increase in value. China is benefiting massively from the global technology investment cycle and specifically in AI. However, Chinese exports of integrated circuits increased by 111.1% in value over the first ten months of the year but by only 3.2% in volume. This divergence reflects an increase in the average value of exported components rather than a comparable surge in the quantities shipped.

📈 Another interesting figure is the 41.6% increase in imports. Some might interpret this as evidence of a real recovery in Chinese consumption but a significant share of these imports is used to supply China's manufacturing sector, especially its technology supply chains. Importing more components to manufacture equipment that will be exported doesn't mean domestic demand is recovering. Domestic consumption remains insufficient to sustain growth on its own and China's cumulative trade surplus has already exceeded $1 trillion over the first ten months of the year, highlighting just how dependent the country remains on foreign demand.

⚠️ This situation could become problematic in 2027. The more China benefits from global AI investment, the more certain segments of its industrial economy become dependent on that spending continuing. If hyperscalers begin slowing their capital expenditure because returns fail to justify the investments, the consequences could spread throughout the entire industrial supply chain, from electronic components to computing equipment. Add to that increasingly demanding base effects and the possibility of escalating trade tensions with the US and Europe. China is becoming simultaneously more powerful industrially and potentially more vulnerable to economic decisions made abroad.

The more China strengthens its global manufacturing dominance, the more its economic growth risks becoming dependent on external demand that it cannot fully control.

For the first time in my career, I'm starting to think a complete rewrite might actually be the right call.

If you're building in AI, the most important thing to master is the economics of compute. My take: respect the GPU or the GPU will humble you.

We're in a compute shortage. A GB300 costs roughly $7/hour on the spot market so depending on the frontier model, that hour buys you some millions of output tokens.

The only question is: how much customer value can you create with those tokens?

If it's less than $7, you have a problem. Customer won't pay you, so you won't be able to afford more compute, and VCs can subsidize you forever. Eventually, someone who creates more value per GPU-hour will outbid you.

The same GPU-hour could be spent generating another meme or helping discover a cancer treatment. The economic value of those outputs is wildly different.

My take is that you have to design your entire product around this equation. What's the smallest model that can do the job? Can you batch the work? Run it asynchronously during off-peak hours? Avoid generating tokens you don't need?

Every architecture decision, every feature, every token changes your compute economics. The entire roadmap has to be decided for the compute equation. 

What's hard is that in traditional software eng, you could often treat compute as practically free but the agent era, compute is the most important constraint.
